title: Gimblett Gravels
subtitle: An old riverbed
objectives: Explain why it suits red grapes

steps.title: A river changed course
steps.body: Gimblett Gravels is an area of about 800 hectares west of Hastings. It's the old bed of the Ngaruroro River, which changed course after a flood in 1867, leaving deep, stony gravel. The land was once considered useless for farming and was nearly quarried for gravel.

steps.title: Warm, stony soil
steps.body: The gravel soils drain quickly and store the sun's heat, releasing it at night, making the area a few degrees warmer than its surroundings. Low fertility limits vigour. That helps Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah ripen fully, giving concentrated, structured wines. Irrigation is needed, as the gravel holds little water.

steps.prompt: Why does Gimblett Gravels suit red grapes?
options: Stony soil drains and stores heat

steps.title: A defined district
steps.body: In 2001, producers created the Gimblett Gravels Winegrowing District, defined by soil type rather than political boundaries, a rare approach. Wines labelled Gimblett Gravels must come at least 95% from the district. The Bridge Pa Triangle, nearby, is another warm, red-focused sub-area.

steps.explanation: It's low in fertility and drains fast.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Gimblett Gravels is an old riverbed left by an 1867 flood
Stony soil drains and stores heat for red grapes
Its district, from 2001, is defined by soil
